title: Maximize the Topmost Element After K Moves
statement:
The array `nums` describes a pile, listed from the top down: `nums[0]` is on top. You must make **exactly** `k` moves, and each move is one of these:

- take the top element off the pile (only when the pile has something on it);
- put back any one element that was taken off earlier, which then sits on top (only when something has been taken off).

Return the largest value that can be on top of the pile once all `k` moves are done. If every possible sequence of `k` moves leaves the pile empty, return `-1`.
notes:
## Intuition

Simulating every move sequence explodes, so ask instead which elements can possibly finish on top. Two ways exist. Either remove exactly `k` elements, leaving `nums[k]` exposed (possible only when `k < n`), or remove `k - 1` elements and spend the last move putting the best removed one back. In the second case any of the first `k - 1` elements can be chosen; `nums[k - 1]` itself is out of reach, since putting it back needs one more move. When `k > n`, spare moves can be burned by removing and re-adding, so every element is reachable, except with a single element, where moves just alternate between "on" and "off".

## Approach

1. If the pile has one element and `k` is odd, the pile is empty at the end: return `-1`.
2. Let `removable = min(k - 1, n)`: the first `removable` elements can be taken off and one put back last. Track their maximum in `best`.
3. If `k < n`, removing `k` elements exposes `nums[k]`; compare it with `best`.
4. Return `best`. After step 1 at least one of the two cases always applies, so `best` holds a real value.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [5, 2, 2, 4, 0, 6]`, `k = 4`, `n = 6`. `removable = min(3, 6) = 3`, so `best = max(5, 2, 2) = 5`. Since `4 < 6`, `nums[4] = 0` could also be exposed, but `0 < 5`. The answer is `5`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(min(k, n)): one pass over at most `n` elements.
- Space: O(1).

## Pitfalls

- `nums[k - 1]` is never a candidate: removing it and putting it back costs two moves after the first `k - 1`.
- With `k = 0` no move happens; `removable` is `-1` and the answer comes from `nums[0]`.
- A single-element pile with odd `k` is empty at the end; with even `k` the element is back on top.
- With `k === n` every removal would empty the pile, so only the first `n - 1` elements count.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `n` | number of elements in the pile |
| `best` | largest value that can end on top so far (`-1` for none) |
| `removable` | how many top elements can be removed while one move is kept for a put-back |
| `i` | index of a removable element |

narration.2: Count the elements in the pile.
narration.3: With a single element, the moves can only alternate between taking it off and putting it back.
narration.4: An odd number of such moves ends with the pile empty.
narration.7: Up to k - 1 elements can be removed while the last move is saved for putting one back.
narration.8: Visit each element that can be removed and later returned.
narration.9: Keep the largest of them as a candidate for the final top.
narration.11: If the pile holds more than k elements, removing exactly k of them exposes nums[k].
narration.12: Compare the exposed element with the best put-back candidate.
narration.14: Return the largest value that can end on top.
